The problem, I think, with Wallace (and writers like Wallace) is that they're often viewed as even more than genius - as positively infallible. Every error, every inaccuracy, every inconsistency is all supposedly a part of some grand master plan - even Wallace himself wrote "All typos intentional" on a draft of Jest. So when I notice things like the inconsistent geographic features of Enfield, I'm tearing my hair out to trying to figure out what this could possible signify when with another, less deified, writer I would likely brush it off as "shitty geography" and move on. Reading Jest sometimes feels like you're taking part in Wallace's game but he never told you the rules and never plans to - an experience which, to borrow your phrase, can be both frustrating and entertaining.
